summary:
**Dancing with the SARs** is a NISAR-based project focused on monitoring mangrove and wetland changes in the Sundarbans Delta, with Gosaba, West Bengal, as our pilot study area. We are developing a workflow that uses NASA–ISRO NISAR's L-band and S-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations to identify and visualize changes in the Earth's surface, particularly those affecting mangrove ecosystems.

The project addresses the challenge of monitoring environmentally sensitive regions where frequent cloud cover makes conventional optical satellite observations difficult. By analysing radar backscatter across multiple observation dates, we aim to distinguish potential vegetation changes from natural variations caused by tides, rainfall and soil moisture. Our work includes satellite data discovery, product inspection and the development of a multi-temporal processing pipeline, with an interactive visualization platform planned as the next stage.

This project is important because timely, reliable monitoring can support mangrove conservation, ecosystem assessment and better-informed environmental decision-making.
details:
Project Details – Dancing with the SARs

Dancing with the SARs is a satellite-based environmental monitoring project that aims to detect and visualize changes in mangrove and wetland ecosystems using data from NASA–ISRO's NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) mission. Our pilot study focuses on Gosaba Community Block in the Sundarbans Delta, West Bengal, an ecologically sensitive region affected by tidal changes, coastal erosion, flooding and environmental disturbances.

The project works by analysing radar observations collected at different dates. Unlike conventional optical satellites, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) can collect useful observations through cloud cover and during both day and night. We focus on L-band radar backscatter, which can provide information about vegetation structure and interactions between vegetation and water. By comparing observations from the same satellite track over time, our planned processing workflow aims to identify potential changes in mangrove cover and wetland conditions. An important part of the methodology is considering natural variations caused by tides, rainfall and soil moisture so that they are not automatically mistaken for environmental degradation.

The main benefit of this project is its potential to provide more consistent monitoring of vulnerable coastal ecosystems. It could help researchers, conservation groups and environmental authorities identify areas that may require further investigation, support mangrove conservation and improve understanding of changes in wetland environments. Our intended impact is to make satellite-based environmental information easier to interpret and more accessible through an interactive visualization platform.

For development, our team has used Python for data inspection and processing, Jupyter/Google Colab notebooks for analysis, HDF5 tools and libraries for inspecting NISAR data products, Git and GitHub for version control, and NASA's ASF DAAC data archive for satellite data discovery. We have also explored the Bhoonidhi archive for the project's planned S-band comparison. The current work includes satellite data discovery, archive auditing, product structure inspection and preparation of the processing pipeline. Multi-temporal analysis and the interactive web dashboard are planned development stages. The intended dashboard will present mapped changes and supporting observations in an understandable visual format.

The creative aspect of our project is the combination of advanced dual-frequency radar technology with a focused, local environmental application. Instead of treating every change in radar intensity as vegetation loss, we consider the influence of the Sundarbans' dynamic tidal environment. Our team has considered data availability, spatial resolution, satellite observation geometry, consistent acquisition tracks, environmental conditions, scientific reliability and the practical needs of people monitoring mangrove ecosystems. Through this approach, Dancing with the SARs aims to turn complex satellite radar observations into meaningful information for wetland conservation.
